bib.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting", Melanie Sclar, Yejin Choi, Yulia Tsvetkov, Alane Suhr. Venue as stated on every page: "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024". The stamp reads arXiv:2310.11324v2 [cs.CL] 1 Jul 2024. The filename says 2023, but the PDF does not print a v1 date.

COVERAGE: 98,184 of 98,184 chars, all 29 pages, including Appendices A-C and Table 6. References were skimmed for origins. PDF page numbers equal printed page numbers.

CLAIMS
- claim: Formatting changes that preserve meaning can move accuracy by up to 76 points, and by about 10 on average.
  number: 76 points max; ~10 average
  setup: equivalent formats from the authors' grammar; few-shot, 50+ Super-NaturalInstructions tasks, several open models
  quote: "with accuracy varying in up to 76 points for LLaMA-2-13B between equivalent formats, and ∼10 accuracy points on average across 50+ tasks and several models."
  where: p1

- claim: Even 10 random formats give a large spread, and the authors call this a lower bound.
  number: median 7.5 points; top 20% of tasks at least 15 (LLaMA-2) or 9 (Falcon)
  setup: 53 tasks (19 multiple-choice, 34 classification), 10 sampled formats per task, 1- and 5-shot, ranking accuracy, datasets assumed size 1,000
  quote: "a median spread of 7.5 accuracy points across choices in the model and the number of few-shot examples. 20% of tasks consistently result in a spread of at least 15 accuracy points for all LLaMA-2 settings, and at least 9 points for all Falcon settings."
  where: p5

- claim: Changing only the format can reverse which of two models looks better, often with both results statistically significant.
  number: probability 0.141 and 0.140 at d = 0.02; both results significant in 76% and 47% of those cases
  setup: one-sided McNemar tests, p < 0.05, 1000 samples; 53 tasks, 1- and 5-shot (Fig 4). This 76% is not the 76 points above.
  quote: "LLaMA-2-13B and -70B reverse trend by at least d = 0.02 with probability 0.141; LLaMA-2-7B and Falcon-7B reverse trend by at least d = 0.02 with probability 0.140." / "statistically significant (p-value < 0.05) on 1000 samples 2: 76% and 47% respectively for the two model comparisons"
  where: p5

- claim: A format that wins on one model barely tends to win on another, so the authors conclude no format is inherently good or bad.
  number: < 0.62 vs 0.5 chance; table values 57.46%, 55.91%, 61.11%
  setup: format pairs across Llama-2-7b/13b, Llama-2-7b/Falcon, Falcon-7b/7b-Inst
  quote: "there is < 0.62 probability that this trend would hold under another model M ′ (random chance is0.5)"
  where: p16 (Table 3)

- claim: A single atomic change often moves accuracy by 5 points or more, and more so under exact prefix matching.
  number: 24% (prefix matching), 11% (probability ranking)
  setup: 53 tasks, 30 sampled atomic changes each (Fig 6 caption)
  quote: "24% of atomic changes have an associated accuracy change of at least 5 points when using exact prefix matching as scoring criteria (11% when using probability ranking)."
  where: p6

- claim: Single-constant edits can produce extreme gaps, such as removing separators on task280 or changing casing on task322.
  number: task280 0.043 to 0.826; task322 0.614 to 0.714
  setup: probability ranking; Table 2 does not name the model. Selected examples, not typical cases.
  quote: "task280 passage:{}\n answer: {} passage {}\n answer {} 0.043 0.826 0.783" / "task322 COMMENT: {} ANSWER: {} comment: {} answer: {} 0.614 0.714 0.100"
  where: p7

- claim: The API-gated GPT-3.5 model also shows spread, at low cost.
  number: max 56 points, median 6.4, under 10 USD per task
  setup: 320 formats, 53 tasks, budget 40,000 evaluations, exact prefix matching because full logits are unavailable
  quote: "we find a spread up to 56 accuracy points with a median spread of 6.4 accuracy points with GPT3.5 across 320 formats and 53 tasks at a cost of under 10USD on average per task."
  where: p2; detail on p8

- claim: The largest model tested also stays sensitive.
  number: 1-shot median 0.171, max 0.876; 5-shot top quartile 0.310, max 0.841
  setup: LLaMA-2-70B, 4-bit quantization, 40,000 evaluations, 320 formats, probability ranking, 53 tasks
  quote: "yields a median spread of 0.171 (mean=0.221, std=0.200, using probability ranking across 53 tasks; 25% of tasks had a spread of 0.292 or higher, with a maximum spread of 0.876)"
  where: p8

- claim: The scoring metric changes the measured spread, with exact prefix matching giving much higher values.
  number: median 12 to 28 points
  setup: exact prefix matching, per model; the authors say degeneration may partly explain it
  quote: "with median spread ranging from 12 to 28 accuracy points depending on the model used."
  where: p16

- claim: Format affects whether a model gives any valid answer at all, and accuracy tracks that rate closely.
  number: correlation 0.639 to 0.962
  setup: exact prefix accuracy vs "centered mass" (share of outputs matching any valid option); 53 tasks, 10 formats, 1000 samples
  quote: "falcon-7b-instruct 1 0.962 3.6E-289" / "Llama-2-13b 1 0.639 5.8E-61"
  where: p18 (Table 5)

- claim: More shots, larger models and instruction tuning do not remove spread; per-task spreads correlate across those settings.
  number: r=0.83 (7B vs 13B), r=0.43 (Falcon vs Instruct), r=0.82 (1- vs 5-shot); prefix matching r=0.79, 0.32, 0.36
  setup: same task under each pair of settings, Figs 2 and 13
  quote: "there exists significant performance spread regardless of increased model size"; plot labels "r=0.83", "r=0.43", "r=0.82"
  where: p5-6; p17 for prefix matching

- claim: The format space is not locally smooth, so local search is a poor fit.
  number: 32.4% and 33.6% monotonic vs 33.3% by chance
  setup: 24 tasks, 300 triples each, 250 samples, exact prefix matching
  quote: "32.4 and 33.6% of triples were monotonic for multiple-choice and non-multiple-choice tasks respectively. Given that random shuffling within a triple will result in monotonicity 33.3% of the time"
  where: p7

- claim: Thompson sampling estimates spread with far less evaluation than exhaustive search and beats naive sampling and UCB.
  number: within 1 point (Thompson), 4 (naive), 11 (UCB); within 2 points at 5% of the space
  setup: 320 formats, B = 20, 5 trials over 31 tasks (Fig 9); the 5% figure is for 2,500 test examples and 320 formats
  quote: "With a budget of 51,200 evaluations, Thompson sampling results in a spread within 1 accuracy point of the true spread, while naive sampling finds a spread within 4 points, and UCB within 11." / "exploring only 5% of the entire search space for task with 2,500 test examples and 320 plausible formats, we are able to estimate spread within 2 accuracy points of the true spread."
  where: p8; p9

- claim: Sampling more formats raises observed spread, so spread depends on the sample size.
  number: about 17% of tasks gain at least 5 points going from 10 to 20 formats
  setup: 500 formats on 250 samples, 31 tasks, 100 trials (Fig 8)
  quote: "about 17% of tasks are expected to increase their spread by at least 5 accuracy points when increasing from 10 to 20 sampled formats."
  where: p8

- claim: No single feature reliably predicts performance; separators and number formats have the most individual impact.
  number: strongly different in S1 22%, Fitem2 10%, C 1%, S2/Fitem1/Fcasing 0%
  setup: 500 formats, 250 samples each, 31 tasks, 1-shot Llama-2-7B
  quote: "S1 0.132 43% 22%" / "Fitem2 0.173 45% 10%"; "cannot be used to independently predict accuracy changes"
  where: p6-7 (Table 1)

- claim: Formats are readable from the prompt embedding, and that separability correlates moderately with spread.
  number: >=0.98 with top 100 PCs; r = 0.424 (1-shot), 0.555 (5-shot)
  setup: LLaMA-2-7B, 10 formats, 1000 examples, XGBoost, 31 tasks
  quote: "using just the top 100 principal components can result in a classifier with ≥0.98 accuracy in format identification for all 31 tasks analyzed" / "(0.424, p = 8.04 · 10−6; 0.555 for the 5-shot setting; using exact prefix matching)"
  where: p7

- claim: Spread also appears in open-ended generation, though the metrics are noisier.
  number: top quartile ROUGE-L 0.098+, BERTScore 0.09+
  setup: 17 sentence-level tasks, 10 formats, LLaMA-2-7B 5-shot, 50-token limit
  quote: "LLaMA-2-7B 5-shot having 25% of tasks with a ROUGE-L spread of 0.098 or higher, and a BERTScore spread of 0.09 or higher."
  where: p19

- claim: Prompt length does not explain spread overall.
  number: r = 0.228 (prefix), r = -0.022 (ranking); one exception r = 0.559
  setup: all models and n-shots jointly; the exception is LLaMA-2-7B with prefix matching
  quote: "r = 0.228 (p = 1.4 × 10−7) for exact prefix matching metric, and r = −0.022 (p = 0.615) for option ranking metric"
  where: p20

- claim: The authors recommend reporting a range, but say one format is fine for many practical systems.
  number: none
  setup: benchmarks and model comparisons vs practitioners building on an LLM; they also suggest lower-bound reporting for socially impactful tasks
  quote: "choosing a single prompt format that works sufficiently well for use in this larger system is a valid methodological choice."
  where: p9

LIMITS
- Conceded by the authors (App. C, p29): some formats are less likely to be used by humans, such as <sep> or ::. Parsing choices produce odd strings like "amet.; Answer" in "Less than 20% of cases", based on 10 formats across 20 tasks. They restrict to short instructions and inputs and leave input length to future work.
- Conceded elsewhere: spread is only a range (p20). Generation metrics are noisier (p19). Degeneration may inflate prefix-match spread (p16).
- Selection: tasks were filtered, including removal of those at 0% accuracy on LLaMA-2-7B 1-shot, a cap of 4 tasks per original dataset, and a deliberate search for socially impactful tasks (p15). Formats were added to those tasks when absent.
- Scope: only descriptor casing, separators, spacing and enumeration change. Wording, instructions and few-shot examples are held fixed. Results are few-shot only, with no zero-shot arm.
- Comparability: GPT-3.5 uses prefix matching and LLaMA uses ranking, so their medians are not like for like. LLaMA-2-70B was 4-bit quantized.
- My observations, not the authors': no noise floor or confidence interval is reported on spread. Max minus min grows with sample count, as Fig 8 shows. No output-schema or structured-output conditions are tested.
- Dated: the models are LLaMA-2, Falcon-7B and GPT-3.5-Turbo.
- Inconsistency: p9 says embedding separability is "highly correlated" with spread, while p7 says "correlates moderately" (0.424, 0.555). Prefer p7.

BUILDS ON
- Bandit method: Chapelle & Li, 2011 (Thompson sampling); Lai et al., 1985 (UCB).
- UCB setting (c = 2) and gradient-free prompt work: Pryzant et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023.
- Data: Wang et al., 2022 (Super-NaturalInstructions); Honovich et al., 2023 (Instruction Induction).
- Earlier evidence: Aghajanyan, 2023 (tweet, MMLU 6-10 point jump from (A) vs A); Schick et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022 (example ordering).
- Spurious features in other fields: Henderson et al., 2018; Islam et al., 2017; Clark et al., 2011.

CODE
- Repo, not inspected: "https://github.com/msclar/formatspread" (p1, footnote 1).
- Spread definition (p4): "We define the performance spread or simply spread as maxi m(pi, D) − mini m(pi, D)."
- Thompson update (p4, Algorithm 1): "Take θ(t)i from Beta(αi + S(t)i , βi + (N (t)i − S(t)i ))"
- Prior (p14-15): fixed "β = 5" with alpha set from the original format's accuracy. The formula is broken across lines in the extraction, so check it on the page.

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p2: "Slight modifications in prompt format templating may lead to significantly different model performance for a given task." Five formats on one axis, 0.036 to 0.804, 1-shot LLaMA-2-7B, task280. Shows the effect at a glance.
- Fig 3, p6: "Spread across models and n-shots." Box plots show the spread does not disappear across settings.
- Fig 4, p6: probability that M performs worse than M' under another format. Shows reversal against threshold d.
- Fig 6, p8: probability that an atomic change has a given accuracy impact, for both scorers. Shows the metric effect.
- Fig 9, p8: distance to true spread against evaluation budget, for three algorithms.
- Fig 20, p20: accuracy distributions for 30 tasks, showing that a range hides the shape.
- Non-figures worth considering: Table 2 (p7) and Table 6 (p24-28). In Table 6, task280 is 0.84/0.04 on Llama-70B and 0.85/0.80 on GPT3.5, a compact example of model dependence.

PROBLEMS
- pypdf warned "Exceeded 5000 form XObject invocations while extracting text; further form content is skipped." Prose and tables on all 29 pages read continuously, and the skip looks confined to plot content, but I could not identify exactly what was skipped.
- Math is degraded in the grammar (p3), in A.2 (p14, including whitespace values and a dropped index in "Enumerations are indexed from (i.e.,") and in the priors (p14-15). Fig 10 and the plot axes extract as fragments.
- In A.2 the listed S1 and C values appear swapped relative to their definitions: separator-like values sit under C and joiners like "||" under S1. Fig 5 and Figs 22-24 suggest this is either a paper error or an extraction error; I did not check the rendered page.
- Table 3 prints "Falcon-2-7b", probably Falcon-7b. The p8 sentence on 5-shot LLaMA-2-70B omits "or higher". Fig 9 uses B = 20 while Table 6 uses B = 10.
- Fig 20 includes task IDs not in the 53-task list (e.g. task1380, task1431, task309, task903, task729), which implies the 31-task analyses used a different set. The paper does not explain this.
- Spellings "LLMs", "LLaMA", "ROUGE-L", "BERTScore" and "Pryzant" are reproduced as extracted. Quotes join line breaks with spaces.
- No embedded instructions were found.
